Video Title: The Rise of the Machines – Why Automation is Different this Time
Comment Text: The Rise of the Machines offers a nuanced and visually engaging overview of how automation is reshaping economies, jobs, and even our concept of human value. It succeeds in demonstrating that technological change isn’t neutral — it redistributes power, labor, and opportunity. The section showing how machines can now perform not only manual but also cognitive tasks is particularly striking: it challenges the long-held assumption that creativity and judgment belong exclusively to humans.Still, the documentary sometimes leans toward techno-determinism — as if automation’s trajectory were inevitable rather than socially constructed. The reality is that technology doesn’t simply “advance”; it’s steered by political and corporate decisions about investment, regulation, and ownership. Who controls the machines, and who benefits from their productivity, are questions that deserve equal emphasis.The film also hints at universal basic income and lifelong education as possible solutions but doesn’t go far enough in examining the feasibility and ethical implications of these ideas. Can societies sustain dignity and meaning when traditional work declines? What replaces the sense of identity tied to labor?Overall, this documentary is both a warning and an invitation — not to fear machines, but to rethink what kind of future we are programming into them, and who gets to decide.

Comment Text: ### *Chapter 1: Introduction to Cloud Computing**What is the Cloud?* [1, 2]* To understand the cloud, it helps to look at how organizations managed their applications 10-20 years ago [2].* Companies used to buy physical servers from providers like IBM or HP to run their applications [2].* They would store and manage these servers in their own **data centers**, which are physical locations that house servers and networking equipment, complete with temperature controls and wiring [2, 3].*The Problem with Physical Servers* [3, 4]* Physical servers are very expensive and powerful, often coming with high configurations like 100 GB of RAM and 100 CPU cores [3].* If a company deployed a single application that only used 1 GB of RAM and 1 CPU, the remaining 99% of the server&39;s resources were wasted [4].* This inefficiency was very costly, as buying a new server was required for each new application [4].*The Solution: Virtualization* [4, 5]* To solve the problem of wasted resources, the concept of *virtualization* was introduced [4].* Virtualization allows you to create multiple *virtual servers (or virtual machines)* on a single physical server [4].* This way, instead of buying 15 separate servers for 15 applications, a company could buy one powerful server and run all 15 applications on 15 virtual machines on that single piece of hardware [4, 5].* This concept is what makes "the cloud" possible. A developer can request a virtual machine and get access to it via an IP address without knowing where the physical server is actually located [5, 6].### *Chapter 2: Public Cloud vs. Private Cloud**What is a Private Cloud?* [6, 7]* When an organization builds and manages its own cloud infrastructure using virtualization within its own data centers, it is called a *private cloud* [6].* This setup is "private" because it is exclusively used by that single organization; no one from outside can access its resources [6, 7].* System administrators within the company manage this entire environment [6].* Companies in sectors like banking or those handling sensitive information often prefer private clouds, using platforms like OpenStack or VMware to build them [8].*What is a Public Cloud?* [7, 9, 10]* Companies like Amazon (AWS), Microsoft (Azure), and Google (GCP) saw an opportunity to offer cloud infrastructure as a service [7, 9].* They built massive data centers around the world and allow anyone to request computing resources (like virtual machines) from them [9].* This is called a *public cloud* because it is available to the general public. Anyone with an account can create and use resources [9, 10].* The cloud provider (e.g., AWS) manages the physical hardware and data centers, while the user has control over the virtual resources they create [10].*Key Differences:** *Management:* Private clouds are managed by the organization that uses them, while public clouds are managed by third-party providers like AWS, Microsoft, and Google [10].* *Security Concerns:* Some may feel public clouds are less secure because the infrastructure is shared. However, public clouds offer tools like *Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs)* that allow you to create isolated, secure sections within the public cloud for your resources [8, 10].### *Chapter 3: Why is the Public Cloud So Popular?*The popularity of public clouds like AWS is driven by two main factors [11]:1. *Reduced Maintenance Overhead (The Biggest Reason)* * For startups and mid-sized companies, building and maintaining a data center is a huge burden [11]. It requires a dedicated team of experts to manage servers, networking, security, and power 24/7 [11, 12]. * The public cloud eliminates this overhead. Companies can simply create an account and start using resources immediately, allowing them to focus on building their products instead of managing infrastructure [12].2. *Cost (Pay-as-you-go Model)* * Instead of making a massive upfront investment in servers and equipment, public cloud services operate on a *"pay-as-you-go"* model [8, 11]. * This means you only pay for the resources you actually use, which is much more affordable for startups and growing businesses [8].### *Chapter 4: Why is AWS the Most Popular Cloud Platform?** **First-Mover Advantage**: AWS was the pioneer in the public cloud market [13]. They were the first to see the opportunity and successfully create a cloud platform, so many companies began their cloud journey with AWS [13, 14].* **Large Market Share**: Because they started first, AWS has the largest share of the cloud market, followed by Azure and GCP [14].* **More Job Opportunities**: A larger market share means more companies use AWS, which in turn leads to a higher demand for engineers with AWS skills [14, 15]. This makes AWS an ideal platform to learn for anyone starting their cloud career [15].* **Vast Service Offerings**: AWS started with a few services like virtual machines (EC2) and storage, but today it offers over 200 services [12, 16]. They continuously add new services based on market trends, such as managed Kubernetes clusters, to simplify complex setups for their users [16].### *Chapter 5: Are Companies Moving Away from the Cloud?** You may have heard of a trend called *"cloud repatriation,"* where some companies move from the public cloud back to their own private cloud or on-premises data centers [17].* This is true, but it&39;s happening on a very small scale—only about *1-2% of users* are moving back [17].* The reasons for moving back can include security concerns or failing to achieve expected cost savings [18].* However, the overall trend of companies moving to the public cloud continues to grow, especially for startups and mid-sized businesses that cannot afford the cost and maintenance of their own data centers [18, 19]. Therefore, it is still a great time to learn about cloud platforms [17].### *Chapter 6: How to Create an AWS Account*Here is a step-by-step guide to creating your own AWS account to use for learning [19]:1. *Start the Process**: Go to your browser and search for "AWS sign in" [19]. On the sign-in page, click on **"Create new AWS account"* [20].2. **Provide Email and Account Name**: Enter your email address (this will be your "root user" email) and choose an AWS account name. The account name can be changed later [20].3. **Verify Your Email**: AWS will send a verification code to your email. Enter that code to proceed [20, 21].4. **Create a Password**: Set a strong password for your account [21].5. **Enter Personal Information**: * Select *"Personal"* for the account type [21]. * Provide your full name, phone number, country, and address [21, 22]. This information is for billing purposes and doesn&39;t have to be 100% precise, but basic validations (like phone number length) are checked [22].6. **Provide Payment Information**: * You must provide a valid *credit or debit card* [22]. This is for identity verification to prevent spam and ensure you are a legitimate user [23]. * AWS will make a small temporary charge (e.g., ₹2 in India or $1 in the US) to validate the card, which will be refunded [23, 24]. * *Important**: AWS will **not* automatically deduct money from your card if you incur charges. You will receive a bill, and if you don&39;t pay it, your account will be suspended [23, 25].7. **Final Steps**: After your payment details are verified, you will complete a few more simple steps (4 and 5) to finalize your account setup [26].Once your account is created, you can use it to follow along with the video series and learn AWS. Be mindful of the free tier limits to avoid unexpected charges [25].

Comment Text: At 2:45:00 i see you had a problem with the %fs when created a directorie. I think I know what happened. The %fs interacts with the Databricks File System (DBFS). The DBFS is a distributed file system that acts as an abstraction layer over your cloud object storage (the things you can see in unity catalog). The %fs interacts with that, and not with the file system of the workspace. To interact with workspace file system you should use %sh or some program language like python (that interacts with both, DBFS and Workspace Files). When you created that directorie you had created not in your "/Workpace/.../folder", but in "dbfs:/Workspace/.../folder"Furthermore, I would like to express my immense gratitude for the content. [24:29]​Off-page SEO: മറ്റു വിശ്വസനീയമായ സൈറ്റുകളിൽ നിന്ന് ബാക്ക്‌ലിങ്കുകൾ (Backlinks) വഴി വെബ്‌സൈറ്റിന്റെ വിശ്വാസ്യത വർദ്ധിപ്പിക്കുന്നത്. [01:00:15]​Technical SEO: വെബ്‌സൈറ്റിന്റെ വേഗത, മൊബൈൽ ഫ്രണ്ട്ലിനസ്, സെക്യൂരിറ്റി (HTTPS) എന്നിവ മെച്ചപ്പെടുത്തുന്നത്. [01:16:45]​3. സെർച്ച് എഞ്ചിൻ എങ്ങനെ പ്രവർത്തിക്കുന്നു? [01:56:01]​Long-tail keywords: മൂന്നോ അതിലധികമോ വാക്കുകൾ (ഉദാ: &39;Best car washing products for luxury cars&39;). ഇവയിൽ മത്സരം കുറവായതിനാൽ പെട്ടെന്ന് റാങ്ക് ചെയ്യാൻ സാധിക്കും. [01:56:44]​5. പുതിയ സാങ്കേതിക വിദ്യകൾ (AEO, GEO, SXO) [02:20:44]​AEO (Answer Engine Optimization): AI അസിസ്റ്റന്റുകൾക്കും വോയ്‌സ് സെർച്ചിനും മറുപടി നൽകാൻ പാകത്തിൽ ഉള്ളടക്കം തയ്യാറാക്കുന്നത്. Comment Text: Very basic and very poor. You have missed the point and the understanding of what Digital Transformation is all about. Digital transformation is the business journey into the new digital economy. Businesses need to focus on 4 main areas and they usually start with ‘Process Transformation’, which brings about opportunities to enhance one’s ‘Business Model’ that enable new powerful differentiators. They also need to be aware of ‘Domain transformation’ ultimately enabling they to compete in new segments never thought possible. But all of this can only be possible if they realise the ‘organisational/cultural’ transformation requirements.In my experience the main problems I see is that businesses just focus on Process Transformation as it improves efficiency ultimately improving profit, and then they stop. The word Digital is VERY important as people need to understand the different types of data. A business that creates an invoice as a pdf hasn’t really thought about the end to end process as that pdf document usually needs a human on the other side to interpret it, or they use document AI. You can scan a document which makes it hard for processes down the line to interpret it or you can digitize a document whereby other applications can access the data.Digital Transformation is all about end to end seamless processes, today most business processes are human to human, digital Transformation will enables you to evolve these processes to human to machine and in some cases machine to machine. To achieve this businesses will need to really understand their data and how to leverage it through every part of their business to maximise shareholder value.

Comment Text: I did something similar for my dust collection automation. My goal was to make a normally de-energized system as simple as possible for wiring. I already had the 120v iVac blast gates on all my tools and used the cheapest I could find light switches to control them. The switches are labeled by tool and reside in one gang box and are oriented so that at a glance, you can see how many are open and try to keep it to one. I also already had a remote control for my dust collector. So, I had a pretty handy system but wanted it to work without any intervention on my part. To make these parts function automatically, I installed miniature ice cube relays with double throw, double pole contacts, on each tool to be served. I bought relays that included indicator lights so if I ever need to troubleshoot, I can do more of it visually. The coil voltage of the relays matches the voltage of the respective tool. I piggy backed onto the tools power on circuit, so when the tool turns on, the relay activates. One set of the relays contacts activates the dust collector contactor while the other pair of contacts activates the associated blast gate (eliminating the need for the light switch controls). I daisy chained the dust collector circuit in parallel, from tool to tool so that I could run a single pair of wires from the closest tool to the dust collector. This circuit operates in parallel with the existing dust collector remote so I can still use the remote anytime I need dust collection for something without a blast gate. This worked well as all the tools I have on the system are lined up in the same space. The only difference in operation to what you have is that I need to leave the tool run 5 seconds after I&39;m done using it, but I have found I already do this anyway as I always inspect what I just cut/sand either visually or by measuring, before I shut off the tool off (exception would be the compound miter saw). So, the system operates like yours but has no power consumption when not in use. This method prolongs component life and makes the system about as simple as humanly possible. For me, it was also a way to utilize as much of the things I already had in place without having to go buy more stuff.

Comment Text: One pattern worth adding to this stack when building "boring" CRM workflows in n8n: the MySQL node&39;s Execute SQL operation with Query Parameters is your safeguard against injection, since n8n sanitizes values passed as $1, $2 placeholders before they hit the database. The Update operation works great for single-column keys but breaks silently on composite primary keys (like customer_id + product_id), so switching to Execute SQL with a manual WHERE clause is the correct pattern there. Also worth knowing: MySQL DECIMAL values come back as strings by default in n8n to preserve precision, so you need to either enable "Output Decimals as Numbers" explicitly or chain a Set node with toFloat(). Small details that save hours of debugging when the workflow hits production data.

Comment Text: I strongly appreciated the trade-offs and the architecture insights discussed:1. A hybrid approach combined Spark Streaming versus Apache Flink as distributed computing platforms, based on latency criteria for clickstream metrics. The justification being that Apache Spark streaming works well with >= 1 second metrics generation, whereas Apache Flink meets single millisecond / sub-second performance.2. To use the push model ( agents and daemons ) versus the pull model ( the infra ) for large-scale data pipelines : the former being better for real-time needs ( even if it may overwhelms the pipeline ), whereas the latter is polling based and may fail to deliver real-time ( or close-enough-to-real-time ) customer behavior insights.3. The justification for using a NoSQL DB versus a SQL DB for compute storage : NoSQL being schema-less, high-performant, and having low-latency reads and writes - and thus, able to handle large event volumes under ingestion ( e.g. Kafka&39;s 50,000 events / second ), and how he identified the RDBMS storage as a potential pipeline bottleneck.

Video Title: Don&39;t build more AI agents until you watch this
Comment Text: For the past six-months I&39;ve been banging on about using fine-grained specialist agents. If there is anything in an agent&39;s context that it doesn&39;t need, then it will raise the chances of unwanted behaviour and increase the cost of running that agent. I discarded skills within a day or two of their release because they permanently pollute a context (and it&39;s impossible to give them a unique context), and replaced then with very fine grained subagents. Subagents run in their own context and are used a little bit like subroutines - you pass them just enough information to do their job, and ask for a specific minimal amount of information to be returned to the main agent&39;s context.For example, I work in the platform space, so I have agents that &39;operate&39; kubernetes for me. One of them is a "boss" agent that can do deployments. The boss tries a deployment, which might fail, and if it does the boss must work out why so that it can be fixed. To do this, it invokes a diagnostics agent. The diagnostic agent knows about &39;kubectl&39; - a command line program that can control kubernetes. The diagnostics agent has the usual preamble, but then it contains a table of kubectl commands it can use to diagnose problems in kubernetes, along with a description, what the command is used for, and what circumstances it is useful in. In total, there are about 20 commands listed and each one takes up a single line in a markdown file. In total, it has one tool, the terminal, so it cannot delegate any further. It is invoked with a context that contains something like, "The cert-manager deployment seems to have failed. Here&39;s the error message, return a paragraph or two explaining what the cause of the failure is". With its tools it can look at the state of the kubernetes resources, work out what went wrong, and tell me. The diagnostics agent effectively &39;caches&39; the kubectl commands, because it doesn&39;t ahve to look them up at runtime. The boss agent that invokes the diagnostic agent just gets back a short report on what went wrong and why, but it doesn&39;t get the 3000 lines of terminal commands and output it took to get that report. My boss agent doesn&39;t need to even know that kubectl exists. It doesn&39;t need to use the terminal. It doesn&39;t need to have all the diagnostics use-cases embedded within it. This means that my boss&39; context is smaller, faster, and less expensive to run. It also means that my boss&39; context window isn&39;t consumed by a side-quest.

Video Title: Microsoft&39;s CEO says SAAS IS DYING
Comment Text: In an agent driven world where systems interact via MCP, what disappears is the click heavy UI layer, not the core backend. The real value shifts to the structured system of record: canonical data models, permissions, workflows, and auditability. Agents don’t need forms, dashboards, or manual navigation. They operate directly on well defined data and logic through APIs or MCP interfaces. That means your structured data still lives in a reliable backend, typically a relational database like PostgreSQL, while optional layers like vector stores handle unstructured context. The new architecture becomes database + policy engine + workflow runtime + agent interface, with human UI as a thin optional layer. So SaaS is not replaced, it evolves from software humans operate to software that agents operate, with humans supervising exceptions, and the moat shifts from UI to data integrity, schema design, and operational logic.

Video Title: You NEED to STOP Using ChatGPT Right Now
Comment Text: Based on my personal experience with LLMs (I use the main ones like GPT, Grok, and Gemini), I always take everything it says with a grain of salt, from minor grains, to huge grains. When I ask one LLM a question, I also open the other two at the same time and ask them the same questions, to see how well their responses aligned with each other. I found out that the results varied not only in accuracy, but also in presentation. With detailed prompts, I found that said LLMs would also output the same mirroring responses, down to the last level of detail using specific terminologies. This meant that sycophantic behavior itself is inherently present in ALL LLMs, regardless of where they come from. What is interesting though, is that a prompt containing both a yes and a no in the same sentence (some level of ambiguity allowed, not only "please agree with me and tell me it&39;s right", or "please tell me it&39;s wrong") actually yielded a more reasonable, neutral response that both partially agrees with me on what points of the prompt it thinks is right, while also pushing back on the points it deems inaccurate with its database and search results (or unproven). This means that to a certain extent, this sycophantic behavior can be used to our advantage, so long as the prompts we ask of it do not have absolutes in it. Examples of taking advantage of sycophantic behavior with GPT:Ask it about an opinion on a certain topic, what your perspective is, what you think it might be regardless of what your personal opinion is, and tell it not to sugarcoat anything. It will generally output a slightly more grounded answer, but still most likely favored to make you feel better. Do this often enough however, and the way it responds also starts to shift into this, no nonsense, zero flattery behavior.Tl;dr:LLMs are all yes-men, that is a fact. We can however, find a silver lining by using the sycophantic nature to our advantage. If it mirrors our personality? Be blunt and tell it exactly what parts you need, what parts you don&39;t, and tell it specifically not to sugarcoat answers.

Comment Text: Nice tutorial! While I&39;m not the target audience (2.6k hours just on my main account, probably another 1k on friends, and plenty on kee before steam), I still enjoyed going through everything again just as a refresher. I think there are a couple things I&39;d like to add that can help a lot.1. Larger family bore means a physically larger and heavier engine, as well as increasing material costs, but it also raises the power the engine can take relative to a square or undersquare engine of the same displacement. Very useful in the early days, when you&39;re stuck with lower quality internals. Deboring an engine variant also helps in this regard.2. When it comes to carbs, pay close attention to the reliability cons of each type. Single barrel carbs might be kinda dog at everything, they are dirt cheap in cost and engineering, and are very reliable. Single barrel eco carbs offer a bit more efficiency, but with higher costs and lower reliability. Two barrel carbs are a very nice mix of performance and cost. 4 barrel carbs and DCOE are excellent for maximizing performance or efficiency, but are costly and least reliable. In many situations, consider using a pair of lesser carbs as opposed to a single, more advanced carb option. Generally speaking, you can tune the engine in others was (especially carb sizing) to achieve whatever your goal is.3. Single point EFI is awesome. It&39;s dirt cheap and very reliable. While it doesn&39;t serve the best for maximum economy or maximum performance, it&39;s quick engineering times means it can help you meet emissions compliance quickly. EFI engines can utilize the lambda emissions tuning slider! when carbs can not This is very helpful for meeting emissions.4. Different valve configurations have different reliability ratings, which change over time. Early game, pushroad and direct acting OHC engines have a higher base reliability than other configurations. A 2v DOHC will be noticeably more reliable than a 4v DOHC engine. Do not feel like you need the most advanced head technology, especially at the beginning of the game. Those better options will have a lower penalty as time progresses. 5. Once you have an engine factory equipped with a forge works, it&39;s a good idea to run forged conrods and pistons along with your cranks. Light forged pistons are excellent in pretty much every application, and typically deliver only slightly worse fuel economy or emissions than low friction or hyperretectic cast do. If a malicious actor engages in "name squatting" or uploads a package with a slight typo (like spelling "is odd" with a zero instead of an "O"), an AI agent will blindly download and execute it without noticing the difference . Video Title: What I&39;d Learn Instead of Automation in 2026
Comment Text: His thesis has truth inside it, but the packaging is heavily incentive-shaped. He is not neutrally saying, “Here is a balanced analysis of automation careers.”He is saying something closer to: “The old thing you are learning is dying. The new thing is what I teach. Join my ecosystem.” That does not make him wrong, but it does mean the certainty, urgency, and framing should be discounted. The real pattern is not that technical skill disappears. Technical layers do not disappear; they migrate.Hand-stitching became sewing-machine operation. Sewing-machine operation became CAD and pattern software. CAD is now becoming AI-assisted design. But at every stage, there is still a technical layer where people who understand the tool, the system, the constraints, the failure modes, and the business goal outperform everyone else.So the actual lesson is not:“Technical skill becomes worthless.”The better lesson is:“Low-level static technical skill gets commoditized, while adaptive technical skill plus domain judgment becomes more valuable.”His argument also assumes that the rate of technical obsolescence accelerates, but underweights the fact that the rate of learning has also accelerated. Yes, tools change faster now. But people can also learn faster now. AI makes it much easier to learn new tools, understand documentation, debug problems, and move between technical layers than it was 10 years ago.So the winning trait is not “avoid technical learning.” The winning trait is:“Learn technical layers fast, understand the business layer above them, and keep moving up the stack.”This is especially important because his argument also maps very conveniently to what he sells. If he has a paid AI business school or community, then a video saying “automation is dying, learn AI business systems instead” is not just neutral analysis. It is also funnel architecture. The fear hook creates urgency, the thesis creates a worldview shift, and the course becomes the bridge.So I would grade his stance like this:Correct: tool memorization has declining value.Correct: business systems thinking is high leverage.Correct: AI will compress basic automation implementation.Exaggerated: automation is a bad career move.Exaggerated: technical skill becomes obsolete rather than migrating.Biased: his solution maps conveniently to what he sells.The more accurate conclusion is that shallow automation is risky, but adaptive technical ability is still valuable. The goal should not be to become a person who only knows one tool. The goal is to become someone who can quickly learn technical systems, understand the business problem behind them, and use the right tools to create measurable value.

Video Title: The 7 Skills You Need to Build AI Agents
Comment Text: 1- System Design (2:41 - 3:59): You are not just writing prompts; you are architecting an orchestra. This involves designing how LLMs, tools, databases, and sub-agents interact, handling data flow, and planning for component failures. 2- Tool and Contract Design (4:03 - 5:15): Agents interact with the world via tools. You must design airtight contracts (schemas) for these tools. Providing vague schemas leads to "LLM imagination"; precise requirements (like pattern matching and strict types) ensure the agent knows exactly how to interact with external systems. 3- Retrieval Engineering (5:17 - 6:53): Most production agents use RAG. The quality of your retrieval determines your agent&39;s performance ceiling. Skills include optimizing chunking strategies, choosing effective embedding models, and implementing reranking to ensure only relevant information reaches the LLM. 4- Reliability Engineering (6:54 - 8:21): Agents rely on APIs, which inevitably fail. You need to implement standard backend patterns: retry logic with exponential backoff, timeouts to prevent hanging, fallback paths (Plan B), and circuit breakers to stop cascading failures. 5- Security and Safety (8:22 - 9:55): Agents are attack surfaces vulnerable to prompt injections. You must implement input validation to catch malicious requests, output filters to block policy-violating responses, and strict permission boundaries to limit what the agent can actually perform. 6- Evaluation and Observability (9:56 - 11:06): "Vibes" do not scale—metrics do. You need tracing to log every decision and tool call, and evaluation pipelines using test cases with ground-truth answers to measure success rate, latency, and cost before deployment. 7- Product Thinking (11:07 - 12:20): This is UX design for unpredictable systems. You must build trust by designing graceful error handling, setting clear expectations for what the agent can/cannot do, and knowing when to escalate tasks to a human.
Author: @RobertoViegasDutra-t8f6s

Video Title: The 7 Skills You Need to Build AI Agents
Comment Text: As a Stanford Computer Science and Electrical Engineering student with real-world engineering experience, I’ll always stand by this principle:Code understanding requires semantic understanding. That means embeddings, abstractions, architecture, and intent—not simple string matching.Today’s LLMs are probabilistic systems. They’re powerful tools, but they’re not engineers. Too many people fall into the trap of generating mountains of code they don’t understand, hoping AI will somehow reason its way through problems they themselves haven’t fully defined. That approach rarely ships reliable software.AI should be treated the same way programming was treated when it first emerged: as a force multiplier for human capability. Programming amplified writing. AI amplifies programming. Neither replaces the underlying skill.The danger begins when people trade creativity, understanding, and ownership for convenience and confidence. Confidence is cheap. Correctness is expensive.If everyone can generate code, who becomes the chef? The answer is the same as it has always been: the people who understand the ingredients, the process, and the system they are building.Real programmers own their workflows. They own their architecture. They understand the tradeoffs. They know why the code exists, not just what the code says.Gradient descent can approximate patterns, but approximation is not understanding. At least not yet. Human intuition still plays a critical role in connecting abstractions, identifying hidden assumptions, and recognizing when a solution is fundamentally wrong despite looking plausible.When AI becomes truly deterministic, verifiable, and capable of proving its own correctness, we can revisit the conversation about handing over the controls. Until then, architects should architect. Designers should design. Engineers should engineer.Even people like Andrej Karpathy understand this reality. The most effective practitioners are not replacing themselves with AI. They are building better workflows around AI. Agentic systems, evaluation frameworks, guardrails, retrieval pipelines, verification loops, and infrastructure still require deliberate engineering.AI is at its best when it accelerates human judgment, not when it replaces it.Continue burning tokens and funding larger models if you want. Just understand the tradeoff. More generation does not automatically produce more value.Don’t be the monkey with a shotgun aiming at bananas. By the time you’ve blasted every tree in sight, the fruit has already spoiled.Evaluate.Apply.FOCUS.CONTROL.ADJUST.Because in the end, the engineer who understands the system will always outperform the engineer who merely prompts it.

Comment Text: 1. The video is sponsored.Your paste says: “This video was produced in partnership with Polsia.” That means it is closer to an advertorial than an independent documentary. The creator may still be honest, but the setup is designed to make the founder/company look interesting.2. The claims are enormous, but the proof shown sounds thin.“AI agents build companies,” “no employees,” “$30M seed,” “$9.5M ARR,” “AI handled the fundraise” — those are huge claims. But commenters noticed the video apparently shows more founder lifestyle/talking than hard evidence: live product logs, customer dashboards, audited revenue, retention, support tickets, code diffs, working businesses, etc.3. The branding is deliberately troll-ish.“Polsia” backwards is basically “AI slop.” That makes it feel like the founder is partly leaning into internet bait. Public writeups also mention the “AI slop backwards” naming angle.4. The language is too perfect for virality.Their own site says things like “AI That Runs Your Company While You Sleep,” “Never Hire Again,” and that Polsia plans roadmaps, ships code, runs ads, replies to customers, closes deals, and posts tweets. That is an extremely broad promise — basically “one tool replaces a company.”5. The numbers mostly come from insiders or promotional sources.True Ventures, an investor, published a very supportive post saying the founder had built an autonomous AI system and had crossed serious ARR as a solo founder. That is meaningful, but it is not the same as neutral verification. The founder’s own LinkedIn post claims the $30M raise, $250M valuation, and nearly $10M run rate. Again: possible, but self-reported.6. “No employees” can be technically true but misleading.Even if there are no payroll employees, the company can still depend on contractors, cloud vendors, model providers, partners, investors, APIs, GPU providers, payment processors, and outsourced help. So “zero employees” becomes a headline, not the full operating reality.7. The ARR story is fuzzy.ARR/run-rate can be a slippery startup metric. It might mean “current revenue pace × 12,” not stable contracted revenue. For a hype-driven AI product, the real questions are: how many paying customers stay, how much churn, how much revenue is recurring, and how much is pass-through or one-off?So the best interpretation is:Real company? Probably yes.Real investors? Seems likely.Real product? Probably some version exists.As autonomous and successful as the video implies? Unproven.It feels fake because it is packaged like: “look, the future has arrived, one guy and AI replaced a whole startup.” But the evidence shown, at least from your paste and public materials, looks more like storytelling + hype + investor narrative than a hard technical audit.

Comment Text: 00:00 — Hook + claim: “Most impactful money lesson,” expects low views; staying to the end = “top 1%.”00:56 — What the video will teach: how to start a SaaS company with no cashflow / no coding skills, pick an idea, get customers, keep them, and scale.01:54 — Why SaaS (vs other models): easier long-term, builds a lifelong skill set; not a “6 months then quit” game.SaaS Fundamentals (why it “wins”)03:00 — Myth-busting: you don’t need huge capital, a big dev team, or to “burn tons of money” upfront.04:20 — Target outcome: build micro-SaaS first (roughly $20k–$50k/month) quickly, repeat, then take bigger swings later.07:24 — Core advantage 1: Recurring revenue: customers keep paying if product works → income snowballs.08:33 — Core advantage 2: Multiples + exits: SaaS can be sold at revenue multiples; ecom/agency often can’t.09:47 — AI timing: current AI wave makes MVP building faster; micro-SaaS is the entry ramp.The “Right” SaaS to Build10:27 — Prefer B2B SaaS: avoid consumer apps (Tinder/Uber) early; B2B is more predictable to sell.13:14 — Find “breakage” in businesses:Waste: they lose money without a fix (e.g., spoiled inventory).Scale blocker: they can’t grow because something is broken (e.g., attribution/tracking).14:33 — Pricing logic: if you create/save them ~$50k/month, charging $2k–$5k/month is easy to justify.Niche Strategy (how to get a moat)15:25 — Niche down hard (3–4 layers): pick businesses with money → niche deeper → become the only option.16:27 — Example ladder: Doctors → Dentists → Organic Dentists (hyper-specific).18:47 — Selling “secret”: not sales charisma—uniqueness + high need (“hot dog stand in a desert”).Go-To-Market (how to win early)20:46 — “Do things that don’t scale”: early advantage = hands-on, custom-fit, 1:1 setups.21:03 — Stripe story: they installed for people for free → users saw value → word-of-mouth + lock-in.22:18 — Build a platform you can “bolt features onto”: a base app + quick custom add-ons per customer.23:38 — Don’t charge upfront at first (in his model): install + get them results → then charge to keep results.24:16 — Use early wins as proof: 2–3 customers → results/testimonials → easier closes for the next ones.Building Options (depending on your budget)28:02 — Option A (you have money): hire a firm (“CTO in a box”), then hire in-house later.28:50 — Option B (you’re broke): learn basics + use vibe-coding to ship MVPs fast.29:00 — Claim: coding isn’t that hard; the “hard path” is competing in saturated influencer/ecom spaces.MVP & Ethics32:25 — MVP definition: minimum version that demonstrates the outcome.32:34 — You can simulate the concept…32:48 — …but don’t fake it as AI / don’t scam (he explicitly warns against that).Cashflow Mechanics (how he suggests funding the early phase)34:40 — Guarantee results: strongest way to acquire customers fast.35:08 — Annual upfront + refund guarantee: get cash upfront to fund build/support; refund if no results.37:06 — “Real business secret”: repeat customers for years = everything; refunds don’t matter if you deliver outcomes.Scaling Path (when to switch modes)39:41 — Early stage = “software agency” vibe: not infinitely scalable, but scalable to $50k/month.40:01 — Later switch to self-serve: once you have ~50 clients + proof, move to signup + instructions.41:00 — Failure lesson (Market Hero vs Klaviyo): Market Hero tried “for everyone” + cheap; Klaviyo focused on Shopify niche and won.Micro-SaaS vs Big-SaaS Reality Check44:43 — Big revenue goals often reduce cashflow: big SaaS competes on valuations and can burn money to win.45:54 — Practical advice: build multiple niche micro-SaaS for cashflow; use experience to build the “big one” later.The best ideas do not come from genius brainstorming. They come from finding real problems inside businesses. These problems either waste money or block growth. Build a small tool that fixes one specific problem and sells a clear result. Focus on B2B, then niche down hard. Pick a market with money and go more specific until competition is low and your offer feels like the obvious choice. In the beginning, do hands on work. Set it up for customers, customize it, and make sure they actually get results. When results are real, selling becomes much easier because the value is clear. Strong guarantees can help because customers feel less risk. Later, once you have proof and stable customers, you can turn it into a more self serve product. Comment Text: This shift from optimizing for keywords to optimizing for the moment behind the search is probably one of the most important mindset changes for marketers right now. More traffic does not automatically create more revenue. Faster response times, stronger follow up, clearer positioning, and consistent conversion often have a bigger impact than another blog post or another SEO tactic. Comment Text: day-3(this is aigenerated ,i am not claming i wrote this)Summary of Today&39;s Lecture – My Understanding What is Amazon EC2? Amazon EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) is a core AWS service that provides scalable virtual servers, known as instances, in the cloud. Instead of buying physical hardware, you can rent a virtual machine that comes with a combination of CPU, RAM, storage, and networking capabilities, all configured to your specific needs. Why do we need EC2? Managing EC2 instances is much easier and more cost-effective compared to maintaining on-premises physical servers. With EC2, you follow a pay-as-you-go model, meaning you only pay for what you use. This eliminates the massive upfront costs and maintenance headaches associated with physical infrastructure, similar to the cloud advantages discussed in earlier lectures. Key Concepts Covered: EC2 Instance Types: AWS offers a wide range of instance types optimized for different workloads: General Purpose (e.g., t2.micro, t3, m5): A balance of compute, memory, and networking. Ideal for web servers, small databases, and development environments. Compute Optimized (e.g., c5, c6g): Designed for high-performance compute tasks like batch processing and high-traffic web servers. Memory Optimized (e.g., r5, x1e): Optimized for memory-intensive workloads like in-memory databases and real-time analytics. Storage Optimized (e.g., i3, d3): Designed for high-speed, low-latency access to local storage. Regions & Availability Zones: EC2 instances can be launched in different geographic regions and availability zones around the world, allowing you to deploy applications closer to your users for better performance and high availability. Security Groups: These act as virtual firewalls for your EC2 instances, controlling inbound and outbound traffic. You define rules to allow specific traffic, like SSH (port 22) or HTTP (port 8080). Key Pairs: Key pairs are used for secure SSH access to your EC2 instances. You download a private key file (.pem) and use it to connect to your instance. Hands-on Project: Deploying Jenkins on AWS The practical part of the session involved a step-by-step project to deploy Jenkins (a popular automation server) on an EC2 instance. The key steps were: Launch an EC2 Instance: Create an EC2 instance using the AWS Free Tier. This typically involves choosing an Amazon Linux 2 or Ubuntu AMI and a t2.micro instance type. Configure Security: Set up a key pair for secure SSH access and configure the security group to allow traffic on port 8080 (the default port for Jenkins). Connect via SSH: Use the SSH command with your key pair to connect to the instance. Install Jenkins: Once connected, update the system, install Java (a prerequisite for Jenkins), add the Jenkins repository, and install Jenkins. Access Jenkins: After installation, access the Jenkins web interface by entering the instance&39;s public IP address followed by port 8080 in a web browser. Comment Text: LmaoI did a travel chatbot pretty much like this. 2 years ago. Each agent had a prompt and produced a .md file that had been sent to the next one, precisely because debugging it was hell*1. First guardrails - filter irrelevant and politically incorrect queries. We do not want our bot to even engage in queries like "I&39;d like to go to a place without Black people", or the chatbot helping kids do their homework.2. Sorting - is this the first entry, what do we know already, what are we missing, is the user done with requirements.3. Extract user requirements.4. Match vs embeddings + generate synonyms (i.e. we had skiing trips where the word "snow" did not happen once, it was "hit the slopes" for example, so both embedding and argument extraction had to synonymize).5. See how many arguments we have - if we know when, where, for whom, what&39;s the activity etc. (so we know everything), we return trips. That&39;s rarely the case, so we categorize requirements we got from the input, to ask for the missing ones.6. Response - reiterate collected requirements + matching deal/hardcoded "no" (for politically incorrect/irrelevant - hardcoded because we really do not want the bot to answer "Armenian genocide is a complex issue", we had a safe and neutral answer that could not be published on twitter)/ a question for more requirements/"we have no matches, do you wish to see partial matches?".It worked until the client started tinkering with the prompts. But the idea was that each stage had to publish a concise input for a subsequent stage, limiting the context. Nothing was actually receiveing the entire conversation, only a so-far summary of it appended as needed. Signal2noise ratio is a bitch.* debugging story: because the agent&39;s tone statement was "to inspire people to travel", it was making up trips that weren&39;t available, i.e. "I want to go somewhere warm this spring" -> "how about crossing Sahara desert on a camel&39;s back under a sea of stars?" -> "sounds good" -> "sorry, we got nothing like it"

Implementing advanced encryption would have forced IBM to build two completely separate domestic and international versions of the software, so a lot of consumer companies just left it unencrypted to avoid the legal nightmare. The rules didn&39;t finally change until early 2000!

Video Title: What it Takes to Build a Tech Startup
Comment Text: Elliott Potter’s talk explains that building a tech startup is less about a perfect idea and more about doing persistent, “unsexy” work, listening to customers, and repeatedly adapting your product and your own role as a founder. ​ Elliott’s path into startups Potter started in Birmingham intending to be a music producer, but a friend pulled him into early-stage Shipt, where he led launches into 63 cities and fell in love with startups and software. Shipt’s rapid growth and sale to Target gave him stock options, which he later used to start Linq. Origin and evolution of Linq Linq began almost accidentally from a side project: an Instagram growth bot whose QR-code checkout flow morphed into a “digital business card” as coworkers kept asking for it. During Covid, they put QR codes and NFC into physical cards ordered from Alibaba, which unexpectedly took off and led to subscriptions (“Linq Pro”) and then a standardized solution for companies (“Linq for Teams”). Finding product‑market fit via customer pull Potter emphasizes that many startups are “solutions looking for a problem” and the real art is balancing creativity with genuine customer problems. Linq kept following user pull: custom card designs, branded profiles, CRM integrations, then finally bundling everything into team products as customers kept asking for those pieces. Pivot to AI phone and messaging infrastructure They next built “Linq Phone,” an AI-powered work number that auto-texted and logged calls to CRMs; users engaged with it far more and paid higher prices than for digital cards. When customers demanded “blue texts” (iMessage) instead of green SMS, Linq created “Linq Blue,” which dramatically improved demo show-up rates and, at a price over 1,000 dollars per year, doubled their annual recurring revenue in eight months. Becoming an API platform A customer then asked to plug directly into Linq’s messaging API rather than use its sales tools, revealing a more valuable “infrastructure” business where others could build AI products on top. Seeing this higher-stickiness opportunity, Potter chose to pivot away from the successful but narrower sales-product line and focus the whole company on being an API platform for messaging in the AI era. Lessons on entrepreneurship and being a CEO He argues success comes from doing hard, messy work others avoid, not premature optimization or chasing only flashy tasks. A good CEO, in his view, must be confident yet humble, willing to be wrong, develop strong pattern recognition and people skills, and repeatedly “reinvent” themselves—doing every job early so they know what “good” looks like before hiring specialists.

And to be fair, Fable itself isn’t nearly as superior as people make it sound.So yeah, there was a massive amount of hype, but no obvious breakthrough. The only genuinely noticeable advantage of GPT-5.6 is that it doesn’t burn through tokens as aggressively. Fable 5 is the undisputed champion of destroying a $200 subscription, and now it looks like they also want to sell additional credits separately. I’m guessing those credits will be ridiculously expensive — and the model still won’t be worth the price.For Anthropic to actually win this competition, they need to make Fable at least three times cheaper. Especially when models like GLM 5.2 already exist — it’s a genuinely interesting LLM, even though it can be completely unhinged sometimes 😂 Kimi 2.7 is interesting too, but waiting two to five minutes for a single response seriously ruins the experience.Chinese models can occasionally deliver extremely impressive results, but when it comes to stability, speed, and consistent quality, using them still feels like a lottery. 😁

If I ask, "What color would look nice on my table?" or "What do you think about this idea?" I expect a creative response based on the model&39;s existing knowledge, not another search.After a while, the conversation starts to feel awkward because almost every topic is interrupted with "checking" or "let me search for that." It no longer feels like a natural conversation. It feels like I&39;m waiting for a search engine instead of talking to an intelligent voice assistant.Please let GPT Live rely on its built-in knowledge for everyday conversations, opinions, storytelling, brainstorming, and common knowledge. Comment Text: AI, Robotics, and the Future of Economic OrganizationMuch of today&39;s discussion about AI focuses on one question: Will AI replace jobs? I believe that is only part of a much larger transformation.The more fundamental question is:What is the optimal size of a productive organization in the age of AI, robotics, and advanced manufacturing?For most of human history, large organizations had significant advantages. Mass production required enormous factories, large workforces, expensive machinery, and complex supply chains. Bigger usually meant lower costs.AI and robotics are beginning to change that equation.As intelligent machines become capable of designing, manufacturing, inspecting, and distributing products with minimal human intervention, the minimum efficient size of a manufacturing company may shrink dramatically. Instead of producing millions of identical products, smaller businesses could profitably manufacture thousands—or even hundreds—of customized, high-quality products.This could encourage a new wave of local entrepreneurship, innovation, and resilience. Communities would no longer need to depend entirely on a handful of giant corporations. Smaller firms could compete by producing durable, repairable, specialized products tailored to local needs.However, technology alone will not determine whether this transition succeeds.Human beings evolved in relatively small groups where cooperation, reputation, and trust were essential. We naturally form tribes, seek status within our communities, and are cautious about rapid change. These tendencies helped our ancestors survive, but they also influence how modern societies respond to technological change.If people believe AI and robotics exist only to eliminate jobs and concentrate wealth, resistance will be understandable. But if these technologies are used to expand opportunity, support smaller enterprises, strengthen communities, and improve quality of life, public acceptance is likely to grow.The challenge, therefore, is not merely engineering. It is understanding human psychology, neurobiology, and our evolutionary history. Successful societies will recognize that technological progress and human nature must evolve together.Another important question is ownership.If AI and robotics are owned by only a small number of organizations, wealth and influence may become increasingly concentrated. But if ownership is widely distributed through entrepreneurs, cooperatives, local businesses, and communities, the benefits of automation could be shared much more broadly.The future is not simply about replacing human labor. It is about redesigning economic systems so that people and intelligent machines complement one another.Rather than asking whether AI will replace us, we should ask how AI can help create a society that is more innovative, more resilient, more prosperous, and more human.Technology provides the tools. Comment Text: The utility-based agent concept is exactly what production AI orchestration needs more of. When you formalize this, each workflow step gets routed to the optimal model + agent combination based on a utility function that balances quality vs cost vs speed. A $0.01 API call to a small model might have 95% of the utility of a $0.30 call to a frontier model for many subtasks. The learning agent type maps perfectly to continuous improvement of these routing decisions - log every workflow execution, measure outcomes, and let the routing policy evolve. Video Title: What is AWS? | Amazon Web Services
Comment Text: “Application” - a BUNCH of lines of code. The logic is 1 line of code is quicker for a computer to calculate than 1000 lines of code. Applications are thousands of lines of code and more. Sometimes it becomes too much for one computer or laptop to run, especially if the application is coded to interact with user inputs (likes, comments, subscriptions, etc). Plus if the application has millions of users, then there needs to be millions of username/passwords that have to be stored, usually these days with phone numbers, email accounts, etc. ..so that takes a lot of “memory” to store that info so the application can refer to it when needed. All of this is usually too much for one computer or laptop at your home to handle. SO what you do is you buy or rent maybe 2/3/10 “racks” or “servers” at a data center. Each one of these “racks” is basically 1 very good computer (just without a monitor). It has a CPU, and GPU, a storage hard drive, and a bunch of RAM (ideally since you’re paying for it). If you buy 2/3/10 computers on a rack in a data center…you can have 2/3/10 computers all working on running your application that has millions of users without failing OR being too slow. When they say everything is connected my “networking”, they mean it’s connected to underground fiber optic cables. Basically all of the instructions to run the application, or “make it work”, can be sent through fiber optic cables which signals the computers instructions by flashing lights. It works like Morse code where a flash of light in a certain time frame means a 1. And if there is no flash of light within a certain time frame that means a 0. And this happens at literally billions of times per second. That’s why when you search for a YouTube video is takes 0.1 seconds to load…it’s very fast because all the instructions travel from your phone/computer, at the speed of light, to the 2/3/10 “servers” you bought, back to your phone

Comment Text: How Augmented Reality Can Change the World Cortney Harding Bold title, I know. And as someone who considers herself allergic to grand, sweeping statements like the one I just made, I understand if you’re skeptical. But the more I turn augmented reality over in my head, the more I think about broader implication beyond selling products and engaging customers (though don’t get me wrong, it’s amazing for that, I want to keep my day job). Augmented reality could lead to a revolution in the way we communicate — and provide a path to inclusion for people with learning challenges and the illiterate. According to UNICEF data, almost 10% of the world’s population can be considered illiterate, and women are disproportionately less likely to be able to read than men. Add to those millions of people, many of whom are in rapidly developing countries, the number of people who struggle with reading and those who are in countries where they don’t speak the dominant language, and the number balloons. Using more contextual and image driven augmented reality applications would allow for these people to participate more fully in society, creating net benefits for everyone. Many refugees and migrants, for instance, lack language skills when they first arrive in new countries, and plenty of them also lack functional literacy as well. If they were able to use smart devices to navigate their lives, they could more quickly be integrated into their new environments, and perhaps learn simple job skills using AR to mimic with work they would be doing. Even if women were prevented from working outside the home, for instance, they could use visual cues to navigate the city and seek resources for their daily lives. In developing countries, AR could be used to lift people out of poverty but providing basic, visually driven skills training, as well as a way to communicate with the wider world. But beyond that, it provides something less tangible but more important — an end to isolation. We live in a text based world right now, and if the text is unreadable, you can’t function to your highest capacity. If you are given a way to navigate the world that is understandable, it will get you out of the bubble and into society, and perhaps give you the confidence to go forth and learn how to read text. Augmented reality will never replace reading, of course, and nor should it. But it can add an extra layer on top of the world to make it more welcoming and comprehensible for some of the most disenfranchised among us, and that’s reason enough to lean in and start experimenting. If just one woman can learn a skill that gives her ability to escape a bad relationship, or one man can learn how to navigate a strange and scary city and feel more included, then that will be enough.

Comment Text: My structure differed a lot from the interviewer&39;s. I came up with it using two minutes exactly. Please let me know if it&39;s on the right track / thought process or not:-------------Essentially, I&39;m looking to answer the question of whether the digitalization is worth the sacrifice on the bank&39;s current liquidity issues or not. This is by comparing two buckets to get this understanding, and then a third bucket for alternatives/opportunity cost.The first bucket is liquidity, the second is digitalization, and the last is alternatives.As far as liquidity, I&39;d like to understand what their position is like; do they have obligations? do they foresee improvements in liquidity in the near future? what is their cash position and cash generation like? And then: why do they have this liquidity problem (don&39;t want a deep dive here, but the answer to this can give context about the bank&39;s position)? And then possible solutions to this, to mitigate the tradeoff of liquidity in case the bank introduces digital banking.As for digitization: what is it exactly they want to do? how large is it? what are the timing requirements? funding requirements? why do they want to do it? what is the urgency of this (ie what happens if they don&39;t do it, or if they delay it)? What are the entry methods to it (outsourcing it, doing it themselves, buying licenses from another bank who already has the infrastructure, etc.)These two questions will gauge the level of risk associated; ie is it worth the tradeoff to do this? or not?Lastly, final bucket is about other alternatives. That is, skip it, wait a bit, raise capital by issuing shares or obtaining debt, partner with another bank to do it, etc.----------------Edit: I guess an invisible "bucket" or more accurately stage/phase in my structure (they&39;re not really in bucket form per se) is synthesis of stage 1 (liquidity) and stage 2 (digitization).. After this, and as a small bucket, is alternatives...In essence, think of my framework as two main areas: 1. liquid vs digital, and synthesis. 2. alternatives.

Comment Text: Core Concepts Chat vs. Agent: While a chatbot functions like a meeting (asking/answering), an AI agent functions like an employee, capable of diagnosing problems, planning, executing, and assessing results (the DATA framework, 0:55-1:44). The Rule of R: Before building an agent, evaluate if the task is Repetitive, Rules-based, and generates a clear Return on time (2:06-2:40). The AGENT Framework Martell outlines a repeatable five-step process to build your first agent: A - Aim for a specific outcome: Define the "why" before the "how" and create a "Definition of Done" (DOD) to measure success (2:52-5:20). G - Give it an identity: Use three files—SOUL (behavior/voice), IDENTITY (role/DNA), and USER (context about you)—to focus the agent’s expertise (5:26-9:29). E - Equip it with context: Feed the agent playbooks or "reverse engineer" from your own history (e.g., studying your past emails to mimic your voice) to avoid context rot (9:30-13:34). N - Narrow the scope: Prevent confusion by keeping the agent&39;s role specialized. Use a Manager Agent to orchestrate sub-agents rather than creating one "mega-agent" (13:42-16:06). T - Trust in stages: Start by reviewing all output, then gradually loosen the "leash" as the agent proves reliable (17:50-20:44). Key Takeaways The goal is to move from doing the work to directing the AI, ultimately "buying back" your time. Use different AI models for different tasks (e.g., Haiku for high-volume sorting, Sonnet for routine work, and Opus/Fable for complex orchestration) to optimize for both performance and cost (16:07-17:27).

Comment Text: It&39;s all about just how flat you can make the power curve in the usable rpm range for race engines imo. Of course this has to do with torque in the fact that power is related, but you shouldn&39;t care about engine torque because that&39;s what a gearbox is for. People have a misconception that engine torque is more useful for towing or moving heavy things. In reality, heavy duty vehicles rely on beefing up the chassis/suspension and using short gearing (for wheel torque) to tow heavier things. Diesel engines are used in heavy duty vehicles because of their higher thermal efficiency, which is tangentially related to the torque that they make per combustion event, but the torque itself doesn&39;t allow them to pull more. You could make a heavy duty vehicle accelerate much faster with a gas engine with a higher hp output, but you would have to add significantly more cooling and it would guzzle fuel.
